title: Numerical and experimental framework for bending elasticity of highly flexible slender structures
authors: Shunsuke Nomura, Satsuki Shibuya, Isamu Hashiguchi, Ryuichi Tarumi, Tomohiko G. Sano
abstract: Slender structures are highly flexible, spanning several orders of magnitude in length scale. Their deformation depends on the slenderness of their cross sections, highlighting that the elasticity and geometry of structures are intrinsically coupled. The deformation of the cross-section becomes significant, particularly when tubes and pipes are subjected to bending, known as the Brazier instability. Although the bending performance of slender structures is quantified experimentally using a canonical three-point bending test, their numerical counterparts remain under-explored because complex contact mechanics must be implemented in simulations. In this study, we develop a computational framework to simulate experimental three-point bending tests using a hybrid material point method (hybrid-MPM) approach, which integrates Lagrangian finite element and Eulerian finite difference frameworks. We adapt our framework to elastic tubes and tape springs as canonical examples that exhibit characteristic bending deformation in which the cross-sectional and lengthwise bending are coupled. The predictions of numerical simulations are validated against desktop experiments and classical theory. The excellent agreement between the simulation and the experiments implies that the hybrid-MPM framework provides a robust computational framework for predicting the large deformation of structures involving complex contact, such as soft robots and deployable structures.
summary: This paper introduces a novel hybrid Material Point Method (hybrid-MPM) framework to accurately simulate the bending elasticity of very flexible structures like tubes and tape springs. The methodology successfully couples cross-sectional and lengthwise deformations, allowing for robust prediction of mechanical response under complex contact conditions. Validation against physical experiments confirms its utility for modeling soft robots and deployable systems.
main_problem: The study aims to develop a robust computational framework to simulate the complex, large-deformation bending elasticity of highly flexible slender structures.
main_result: The developed hybrid-MPM framework shows excellent agreement when validating numerical simulations against desktop experiments for both tubes and tape springs.
method: A hybrid Material Point Method (hybrid-MPM) is employed, integrating Lagrangian finite element and Eulerian finite difference frameworks to handle complex contact mechanics during large deformation analysis.
model_or_system: The physical systems studied are slender structures like tubes and tape springs, whose bending behavior exhibits coupling between cross-sectional deformation (e.g., ovalization) and lengthwise bending, particularly near instability points like the Brazier instability.
key_observables: Bending moment (M), applied force (F), displacement ($\Delta$), curvature ($\kappa$), and the resulting force-displacement curve.

main_assumptions: Theoretical derivations assume linear constitutive laws and inextensible centerlines; computationally, the framework is validated against experimental measurements.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares experimental snapshots of bending tests on tubes and tapes with corresponding simulation results. Figure 4 compares force-displacement curves for tape springs across experiments, simulations, and theory.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the theoretical moment-curvature relations via energy minimization, extends this to include internal pressure effects, implements a computational framework using hybrid-MPM, and validates this approach by comparing simulation results against physical three-point bending tests on fabricated samples.
why_interesting: While focused on classical mechanics, the development of advanced numerical techniques like hybrid-MPM for large deformation and contact mechanics is highly relevant to simulating complex geometries encountered in quantum device modeling or soft matter systems where continuum assumptions break down.
